why.correct: Rank the liquids by heat of vaporization: water, methanol, acetone, hexane. The two at the top are exactly the two that hydrogen-bond, which is what you expect if escaping molecules must break hydrogen bonds. The other statements each fail on at least one pair of liquids.
options: Correct. Water (2,260 J/g) and methanol (1,100 J/g) are the two hydrogen-bonding liquids and the two highest values; acetone and hexane are far lower.
Hexane boils at a higher temperature than methanol (69 °C versus 65 °C) yet needs less than a third of the energy per gram to vaporize, so the two do not rise together.
Acetone is polar and hexane is nonpolar, but hexane's specific heat (2.26 J/g·°C) is higher than acetone's (2.15 J/g·°C).
Water has both the highest specific heat and the highest surface tension, the opposite of this pattern.

why.correct: Hydrogen bonds explain why water and methanol stand far above the other two. The acetone-hexane comparison is small and runs against polarity, so another, weaker attraction must also contribute. The best conclusion keeps the main explanation and admits its limit.
options: Correct. Hydrogen bonding separates water and methanol from the other two by a wide margin, but some other attraction (one that grows with molecule size) lets hexane edge out acetone. A good claim fits the large pattern without overreaching.
Hexane has only C–H and C–C bonds, which are nonpolar; with no δ+ hydrogen on O or N, it has nothing that can form hydrogen bonds.
One pair of liquids cannot support a general rule, and the table contradicts it: polar water and methanol attract far more strongly than nonpolar hexane.
Published values for common liquids are reliable. When data disagree with a simple rule, the better move is to refine the explanation, not to throw the data out.

why.correct: heat = mass × heat of vaporization = 900 g × 2,260 J/g = 2,034,000 J = 2,034 kJ. Evaporation removes heat because each escaping molecule must break its hydrogen bonds, taking energy from the skin.
Heat removed = mass × heat of vaporization. Holding heat constant, mass is inversely proportional to the heat of vaporization: 2,260 ÷ 1,100 ≈ 2.1, so about twice as much methanol.
options: Evaporating easily means it evaporates faster, not that each gram carries more heat. Per gram, methanol removes less than half as much heat as water.
Both hydrogen-bond, but water forms more bonds per molecule; the table shows water needs about twice the energy per gram.
Correct. Water removes 2,260 J per gram and methanol 1,100 J per gram, so methanol needs 2,260 ÷ 1,100 ≈ 2.1 times the mass for the same heat.
Surface tension measures cohesion at the surface, not the energy needed to vaporize a gram; the heat of vaporization column is the relevant one.

why.correct: Surface tension comes from cohesion: how strongly surface molecules are pulled by their neighbors. Water can form up to four hydrogen bonds per molecule; methanol, with one O–H and a nonpolar end, forms fewer, so its cohesion is weaker.
options: Methanol's O–H group is polar, but the molecule carries no full charge; and polarity alone does not explain the difference, since acetone is also polar and has similar surface tension to methanol.
Water (18 mass units) is smaller and lighter than methanol (32), so size cannot explain water's stronger cohesion.

Correct. Two δ+ hydrogens and a δ− oxygen let water bond in every direction; methanol has one O–H hydrogen and a nonpolar CH<sub>3</sub> end that cannot hydrogen-bond, so cohesion at its surface is much weaker.
Molecules of a liquid are not covalently bonded to one another; the attractions between them are hydrogen bonds and weaker forces.

why.correct: Read each curve for its lowest point and for when it starts to rise. Acetone has the deepest minimum (7.4 °C at 3 minutes) and is the first to turn upward, as its cloth dries at about 3 minutes.
options: Correct. Acetone fell to 7.4 °C by minute 3, below every other liquid, then rose from minute 4 as the cloth dried.
Water's lowest reading was 16.0 °C, the smallest drop of the three liquids. A high heat per gram does not guarantee the biggest drop.
The lowest readings differ a lot: about 7 °C for acetone, 11 °C for methanol and 16 °C for water.
By minute 8 the methanol thermometer was back up to 18.6 °C, while the water thermometer was still at 16.0 °C.

why.correct: The temperature drop depends on how fast heat is removed. That equals the heat per gram times the grams evaporating each minute. Acetone's weak attractions let it evaporate many times faster, so its cooling rate was highest even though each gram carried less heat.
options: All the cloths started at 22 °C. Specific heat affects how much a substance's temperature changes per joule; it does not explain why evaporation cooled the thermometer more.

Correct. Cooling rate = grams evaporated per minute × heat per gram. Acetone's 2.0 g was gone in about 3 minutes; water had lost only 0.9 g in 8 minutes. The much faster evaporation outweighs the smaller heat per gram.
Acetone has no H on O or N, so it does not donate hydrogen bonds, and forming bonds releases energy rather than absorbing it.
It removed less: 2.0 g × 500 J/g = 1,000 J, versus 0.9 g × 2,260 J/g ≈ 2,030 J for the water. It removed its smaller total in a much shorter time.

why.correct: Each cloth held 2.0 g. Methanol: 2.0 g × 1,100 J/g = 2,200 J. Acetone: 2.0 g × 500 J/g = 1,000 J. Difference: 2,200 − 1,000 = 1,200 J. Acetone gave the deepest drop but removed less heat overall.

A comparison setup that matches the others in every way but one lets you credit a difference to that one factor. Here the one factor is the evaporating liquid; the dry cloth stayed at room temperature, so the drops in the other three are due to evaporation.
options: The dry cloth's reading stayed at 22 °C, so the cloth and fan cause no cooling; that is what the dry cloth was there to check, not something it was expected to show.
A thermometer reads temperature, not the amount of vapor in the air.
The dry cloth holds no liquid; its job is to show what happens with everything the same except evaporation.
Correct. The dry setup is identical except that nothing evaporates. Its steady 22 °C shows that the cooling of the other three comes from evaporation.

why.correct: Humidity slows the rate of evaporation, not the energy each gram takes. Less evaporation per minute means less cooling per minute (a higher lowest temperature) and a cloth that stays wet longer; the heat per gram is unchanged.

variables.name: Lowest temperature the water thermometer reaches
variables.why: Slower evaporation removes heat more slowly, so the thermometer cools less and its lowest reading is higher (closer to 22 °C).

variables.name: Time until the water cloth is dry
variables.why: Fewer grams evaporate each minute, so the 2.0 g of water lasts longer.

variables.name: Heat removed per gram of water that does evaporate
variables.why: The heat of vaporization is a property of water: each gram that evaporates still has to break the same hydrogen bonds, whatever the humidity.

why.correct: The pH fell from 7.00 to 3.00, a drop of 4 units. Each unit is a factor of 10, so [H+] rose by 10 × 10 × 10 × 10 = 10<sup>4</sup> = 10,000 times.

A buffer pair has one member that takes up H<sup>+</sup> (bicarbonate) and one that can release it (carbonic acid). Added H<sup>+</sup> joins bicarbonate, so the free H<sup>+</sup> concentration, and so the pH, changes little.
options: Correct. HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> + H<sup>+</sup> → H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> removes free H<sup>+</sup>. Because pH depends on free H<sup>+</sup>, Beaker B's pH fell by only 0.45 units while Beaker A's fell by 4.68.
The same acid adds the same number of hydrogen ions per milliliter to each beaker, as the setup states. The difference is what happens to them after they are added.
Carbonic acid is an acid: it can release H<sup>+</sup>, not hydroxide. The H<sup>+</sup>-absorbing partner of the pair is bicarbonate.
Both beakers are full of water. If water itself absorbed the ions, Beaker A would have resisted the change too.

why.correct: A buffer has a limited capacity. Each H<sup>+</sup> it absorbs uses up one bicarbonate. When the bicarbonate is gone, the solution behaves like unbuffered water and the pH falls quickly.
options: Correct. Once bicarbonate is used up, nothing absorbs the added H<sup>+</sup>; by 25 mL Beaker B's pH (2.40) is about where Beaker A was after only 2 to 5 mL.
Added acid pushes the pair the other way, turning bicarbonate into carbonic acid, not back. The sharp drop comes from added H<sup>+</sup> that no bicarbonate is left to absorb.
The same 0.10 M acid was used throughout. Each milliliter added the same amount of H<sup>+</sup>.
25 mL of acid only dilutes 100 mL by a fifth, and Beaker A shows that dilution alone does not cause sudden drops. A buffer stops working when one member of the pair is used up.

why.correct: To refute a claim, look for data that contradict it directly. A buffer that held pH near 7 for any amount of acid could not fall to 2.40; the drop after 15 mL shows the bicarbonate ran out.
options: This describes the unbuffered beaker. It contrasts with Beaker B but says nothing about Beaker B's limit.
A drop of 0.11 is small; it supports the idea that the buffer resists change rather than refuting it.
Correct. A drop of more than 3 pH units, ending far from 7, shows the buffer's resistance has a limit.
The starting pH tells you nothing about how each beaker responds to added acid.

why.correct: Opposite charges attract. Water's δ− oxygen end turns toward a cation such as Na<sup>+</sup>, and its δ+ hydrogen end turns toward an anion such as Cl<sup>−</sup>. These shells of water pull the ions out of the crystal.
options: Correct. The δ− oxygen is attracted to the positive Na<sup>+</sup>; the δ+ hydrogens are attracted to the negative Cl<sup>−</sup>.
This reverses the charges. Hydrogens carry δ+ and would be repelled by positive Na<sup>+</sup>.
The ions are surrounded and held by attractions between charges; no electrons are shared and the ions stay as ions.
Full charges attract water's partial charges even more strongly, so the nearest water molecules are lined up, not random.

why.correct: Hydrogen bonds hold ice in an open lattice, so it floats and insulates the water below. Remove that and each new ice layer sinks, exposing more water to freezing air; lakes could freeze solid.
options: Sinking ice would cool the bottom, not warm it, and would remove the insulating layer on top.
The surface cools first, but if new ice sank, the next layer of water would be exposed to the cold air and freeze in turn.
Correct. Floating ice insulates the water below it. Ice that sank would keep exposing new water to the cold air, so the lake could freeze from the bottom up.
Density does not make ice hold heat; the key is that sinking ice would no longer form an insulating lid.

why.correct: Closing stomata cuts transpiration. That removes the evaporation pull that lifts water through the xylem and the evaporative cooling that keeps leaves near air temperature. Water's hydrogen bonds themselves are unchanged.

variables.name: Rate at which water moves up the xylem
variables.why: Transpiration provides the pull. With the stomata closed, less water evaporates from the leaves, so less water is drawn up the cohesive column.

variables.name: Temperature of the leaves
variables.why: Less evaporation means less evaporative cooling, so the sun-warmed leaves heat up.

variables.name: Strength of each hydrogen bond between water molecules in the xylem
variables.why: The strength of a hydrogen bond depends on water's polarity, which closing the stomata does not change; only the number of molecules being pulled up changes.

why.correct: Like dissolves like: ions and polar molecules (salt, methanol) are hydrophilic and dissolve; molecules made only of carbon and hydrogen (oil, wax, hexane) are nonpolar and hydrophobic.
options: Dissolves. Water's partial charges surround and separate the Na<sup>+</sup> and Cl<sup>−</sup> ions.
Does not dissolve. C–H bonds are nonpolar, so oil is hydrophobic and separates into a layer.
Does not dissolve. Wax is even more nonpolar than oil, so water bonds to itself and pushes the wax aside.
Dissolves. Its polar O–H group hydrogen-bonds with water, and the molecule is small.
Does not dissolve. It has no partial charges for water to attract.

why.correct: The bigger the difference in electronegativity between two bonded atoms, the more unequal the sharing. Oxygen pulls far harder than hydrogen, so O–H is the most polar of these bonds.
options: Carbon and hydrogen have similar electronegativity, so C–H bonds are nearly nonpolar.
Correct. Oxygen is much more electronegative than hydrogen, so O–H is strongly polar.
Two identical atoms pull equally, so the sharing is even and the bond is nonpolar.
Two identical atoms share electrons equally.

why.correct: A hydrogen bond needs opposite partial charges: a δ+ hydrogen (bonded to O or N) and a δ− atom such as oxygen on another molecule. Like charges, H to H, repel.
options: Two δ+ hydrogens carry the same partial charge, so they repel rather than attract.
Hydrogen bonds are much weaker than covalent bonds, which is why they are drawn dashed.
Correct. The attraction is between opposite partial charges, so a hydrogen bond runs from the hydrogen of one molecule to the oxygen of another.
The bond between a hydrogen and its own oxygen is covalent. Hydrogen bonds link different molecules.

why.correct: Read down the sulfur-35 column: 93% in proteins. Sulfur is part of some amino acids (such as cysteine), so proteins are where most of a cell's sulfur ends up.
options: Correct. 93% of the sulfur-35 taken up was in the protein fraction, far more than in any other.
Less than 1% of the sulfur label was in nucleic acids, and the small-molecule fraction that includes ATP held only 2%.
The distribution is very uneven: one fraction holds 93% and none of the others holds more than 3%.
Carbohydrates held 1% of the sulfur label. Carbon-14 was common in carbohydrates, but sulfur was not.

why.correct: A tracer marks where its element goes. Phosphorus-32 in the lipid fraction means some lipid molecules contain phosphorus, as phosphate groups. It does not tell you how many lipids do.
options: Correct. The label can only be in a fraction if molecules in that fraction contain phosphorus atoms; in lipids, phosphorus is carried in phosphate groups.
Cells rearrange atoms into new molecules but do not turn one element into another; a phosphorus atom stays phosphorus.
The nucleic acid fraction held 57% of the label, far more than the lipids, and these data say nothing about later use.
The data show where phosphorus went, not what share of lipid molecules contain it; many lipids, such as fats, contain no phosphorus.

why.correct: Match each molecule family to its elements. Carbohydrates and most lipids need only C, H and O; proteins (amino acids) and nucleic acids need N. Without N, the N-containing molecules cannot be made.
options: Every amino acid contains nitrogen, so protein building is limited just as nucleic acid building is.
Correct. Sugars and fats are built from C, H and O, available from carbon dioxide and water. Proteins and nucleic acids contain nitrogen, which is missing.
Sugars contain no nitrogen, so the algae can go on building them from carbon dioxide and water by photosynthesis.
Elements are not interchangeable; amino acids need nitrogen in their amino groups and phosphorus cannot take its place.

why.correct: 17% of 2.40 mmol = 0.17 × 2.40 = 0.408, which rounds to 0.41 mmol.
An isotope has the same number of protons (and so electrons) as the ordinary atom, so its chemistry is the same. Only the neutron count differs, which is what lets researchers detect it.
options: Isotopes are taken up at about the same rate as ordinary atoms; if they were not, they would be a biased guide.
Correct. Chemistry depends on electrons. Isotopes differ only in neutrons, so cells treat them like ordinary atoms, and the label simply marks where they go.
Isotopes differ in neutrons, not electrons; extra electrons would make them ions and change their chemistry.
Damage would distort the results, not make them fair. Labels are useful because they do not change the chemistry.

why.correct: In the light the plant's curve drops from 420 to 285 ppm; in the dark it climbs from 285 to 321 ppm, a much shallower rise.
options: Correct. It fell by 135 ppm in the first 60 minutes and rose by 36 ppm in the next 60.
It fell only while the lamp was on; after 60 minutes it rose.
This is the reverse of the data: 420 ppm fell to 285 ppm in the light.
The rise (about 0.6 ppm per minute) was much slower than the fall (about 2.25 ppm per minute).

why.correct: Two processes run in the plant in the light: photosynthesis (removes CO<sub>2</sub>) and respiration (adds CO<sub>2</sub>). The curve shows the difference. In the dark, photosynthesis stops and only respiration is left, so CO<sub>2</sub> rises.
options: Plants respire all the time, in light and dark. Respiration did not start at 60 minutes; it was hidden by faster photosynthesis.
Correct. Respiration releases carbon dioxide continuously. In the light, photosynthesis removed it faster than respiration added it; in the dark only respiration remained.
The temperature was held at 25 °C, and soil storage would not explain the steady, sustained rise; respiration does.
Oxygen alone has no carbon, so it cannot be turned into carbon dioxide; the carbon comes from sugar broken down in respiration.

why.correct: Change = 420 − 285 = 135 ppm over 60 minutes. 135 ÷ 60 = 2.25 ppm per minute (a fall).

Respiration in the dark: (321 − 285) ÷ 60 = 0.60 ppm per minute. In the light, the measured fall is the net effect: photosynthesis − respiration = 2.25. So photosynthesis = 2.25 + 0.60 = 2.85 ppm per minute.
options: This is the dark rate of rise, the respiration rate on its own, not the photosynthesis rate.
This subtracts respiration from the net fall. But respiration was adding carbon dioxide, so photosynthesis had to remove more than the net fall, not less.
This is the net fall, which is photosynthesis minus respiration. It underestimates how fast photosynthesis worked.
Correct. Net fall (2.25) = photosynthesis − respiration (0.60), so photosynthesis ≈ 2.25 + 0.60 = 2.85 ppm per minute.

why.correct: Combine the rates: crickets +1.2 ppm/min ((564 − 420) ÷ 120), lit plant −2.25 ppm/min. The sum is about −1 ppm/min. The same carbon atoms cycle from cricket to air to plant.
options: The crickets add about 1.2 ppm per minute, while the lit plant removes about 2.25 ppm per minute net, so the plant wins.
They do not cancel: about 2.25 ppm per minute removed versus about 1.2 added.
Correct. Net change ≈ −2.25 + 1.2 = about −1 ppm per minute: carbon atoms breathed out by the crickets are pulled back in by photosynthesis.
The crickets add carbon dioxide; they cannot make the total fall faster than the plant alone could.

why.correct: A sulfhydryl group is –SH. Only Molecule A contains sulfur, and its structure starts HS–.
options: Correct. HS– at the start of its structure is a sulfhydryl group, which is why its formula contains S.
Molecule C carries a carboxyl group (–COOH) on a long hydrocarbon chain; it has no sulfur.
Molecule D carries phosphate groups; its formula has P but no S.
Molecule E carries amino and carboxyl groups but no sulfur.

why.correct: Solubility depends on polarity. Molecule C is almost all CH<sub>2</sub> groups, a hydrocarbon chain, which is nonpolar and hydrophobic. That is the mark of a lipid.
options: A charged –COO<sup>−</sup> group would attract water, not repel it; the group is hydrophilic, not the cause.
Correct. Fifteen carbons carrying hydrogens form a long hydrophobic chain; one polar group at the end cannot make the whole molecule dissolve.
Its two oxygens are in the polar –COOH group; electronegative atoms make a molecule more water-friendly, not less.
Many large molecules dissolve if they are polar; size alone does not decide whether something dissolves.

why.correct: An amino acid has both an amino group (–NH<sub>2</sub>) and a carboxyl group (–COOH). Molecule A has both, and so does Molecule E; containing nitrogen, as ATP does, or a carboxyl group alone, as the long chain does, is not enough.
options: Amino acid. It has an amino group (–NH<sub>2</sub>) and a carboxyl group (–COOH) on the same carbon; it is cysteine.
Not an amino acid. It has hydroxyl and carbonyl groups and no nitrogen: it is a sugar.
Not an amino acid. It has a carboxyl group but no amino group or nitrogen.
Not an amino acid. It contains nitrogen, but in a ring, with a sugar and phosphate groups: it is ATP.
Amino acid. H<sub>2</sub>N–CH<sub>2</sub>–COOH has an amino group and a carboxyl group; it is glycine.

why.correct: Isomers share a formula but differ in how their atoms are bonded. Because structure decides function in biology, isomers can taste, react and fit other molecules differently.
options: Isotopes are atoms of one element with different numbers of neutrons. B and F are molecules, and their atoms are ordinary.
A formula gives only the count of each atom. Moving the C=O changes the structure, so B and F are different molecules.
Correct. Same atoms, different arrangement. Different shapes can behave differently in cells.
The position of a functional group changes the molecule's shape, and shape affects how it interacts with other molecules.

why.correct: Proteins (through their amino groups) and nucleic acids contain nitrogen. Sugars and fats are built from C, H and O.
options: Sugars and fats contain oxygen too.
Carbon is the skeleton of all four families of molecules, sugars and fats included.
Correct. Every amino acid has an amino group, and nucleic acids contain nitrogen too; typical sugars and fats are made of C, H and O.
Sulfur is in some amino acids but not in nucleic acids.

why.correct: Phosphorus goes into phosphate groups, which are part of nucleic acids, ATP and some lipids. A phosphorus-poor soil limits those molecules first.
options: Correct. Both contain phosphorus in phosphate groups, so a phosphorus shortage limits them (and the lipids that carry phosphate).
Amino acids contain C, H, O, N and sometimes S, but not phosphorus.
Carbon skeletons are carbon atoms; sugars are built from C, H and O.
Plants take water in from the soil; they do not build it from phosphorus.

why.correct: Matter cycles. Carbon enters living things when photosynthesis builds sugar from carbon dioxide, moves to you as food, and returns to the air as carbon dioxide from cellular respiration.
options: Living things cannot make atoms. Energy in food is used to rearrange atoms, not to create them.
Correct. Plants pull carbon out of carbon dioxide to build sugar; you got the atom by eating the plant or an animal that ate it.
Organisms rearrange atoms into new molecules but do not change one element into another.
Your cells break down and rebuild molecules constantly, releasing carbon as carbon dioxide; most atoms in a muscle are replaced within months.

why.correct: Functional groups behave consistently: carboxyl groups are acids (lose H<sup>+</sup>), amino groups are bases (gain H<sup>+</sup>), hydroxyl groups are polar, and sulfhydryl groups can bond to each other.
options: Correct. A carboxyl group is acidic: –COOH gives up H<sup>+</sup> and becomes –COO<sup>−</sup>.
That is how an amino group (–NH<sub>2</sub>) behaves, acting as a base.
The C=O and O–H in a carboxyl group are polar, and the group gives up H<sup>+</sup> easily.
That linking behavior describes sulfhydryl (–SH) groups, which can bond to each other.

why.correct: Carbon has four electrons to share, so each carbon atom makes four covalent bonds. That allows long chains, branches, rings and double bonds: a huge variety of skeletons.
options: Oxygen and silicon are far more common in the crust. Carbon's role comes from how it bonds, not how common it is.
Carbon and hydrogen have similar electronegativity, so C–H bonds are nonpolar.
Correct. Four bonds per atom let carbon join other carbons and H, O, N, P and S in an enormous variety of shapes.
Carbon shares electrons; its bonds in biological molecules are covalent.

why.correct: Compare the gain per minute over different intervals: about 1.9 mmol/L per minute early on, about 0.4 near the end. Release slowed but had not stopped by 60 minutes.
options: Correct. In the first 10 minutes about 1.9 mmol/L were released per minute; between 40 and 60 minutes, only about 0.4 mmol/L per minute.
Equal time intervals gave unequal gains: 18.8 mmol/L in the first 10 minutes, but 8.0 in the last 20.
The gains shrink, not grow: 10.1 in the first 5 minutes, 8.0 in the last 20.
The level kept rising after 40 minutes (44.0 to 52.0), and it was still below the 60 mmol/L that full breakdown would give.

why.correct: Change in concentration ÷ time = (18.8 − 0.0) mmol/L ÷ 10 min = 1.88 mmol/L per minute.
Hydrolysis can only happen at a bond that still exists. As more links are broken, fewer remain, so release slows. Water is in huge excess and is not the limit.
options: Correct. As the polymer is cut up, the number of remaining links falls, so each minute fewer bonds are broken.
Each bond broken uses one water molecule, but the tube contains vastly more water than bonds; water does not run out.
If rebuilding matched breaking, the concentration would stop changing, but it was still rising at 60 minutes.
Tube 3 shows the enzyme solution releases no sugar monomers; enzymes are proteins, not sugar polymers.

why.correct: Each comparison tube removes one ingredient. Tube 3 removes the polymer; if monomers had appeared there, some of Tube 1's monomers might have come from the enzyme solution. None did.
options: That question is answered by Tube 2, which has the polymer but no enzyme.
Correct. Tube 3 has the enzyme solution without the polymer and shows 0.0 mmol/L throughout, so the enzyme solution contributes no monomers.
All three tubes were at 37 °C. Testing temperature would need tubes kept at different temperatures.
No tube contains protein as the thing being broken down, so the experiment says nothing about proteins.

why.correct: Hydrolysis: polymer + water → shorter pieces. Bonds between monomers and water molecules are used up, monomers are released, and the atoms themselves are conserved.

variables.name: Number of covalent bonds linking sugar monomers together
variables.why: Each hydrolysis breaks one bond between monomers, so the number of links falls as monomers are released.

variables.name: Number of water molecules in the tube
variables.why: Each bond broken uses one water molecule, so water decreases (by a tiny fraction of the total).

variables.name: Total number of carbon atoms in the tube
variables.why: Hydrolysis rearranges atoms; it does not create or destroy them. The carbon atoms move from the polymer into free monomers.

why.correct: A straight chain of 25 monomers has 24 links, and each link releases one water molecule: 25 − 1 = 24.
Start with 25 × 180 = 4,500 daltons of monomers, then subtract the 24 waters released: 24 × 18 = 432. 4,500 − 432 = 4,068 daltons.
Count links, not monomers. A straight chain of n has n − 1 links; joining its two ends adds one more, so a ring of n has n links and releases n waters.
options: 7 is the count for a straight chain of 8. Closing the ring adds one more link.
Correct. A ring of 8 monomers has 8 links (the chain's 7 plus the one closing the ring), and each link releases one water.
A ring of 8 monomers has 8 links, one per monomer, not 9.
Each link releases one water molecule, not one per monomer per side.

why.correct: Build the molecule one monomer at a time: each new monomer, wherever it attaches, adds exactly one link. So a molecule of n monomers with no rings always has n − 1 links, branched or not.
options: Branches do not remove links; every monomer still needs to be attached to the molecule.
Correct. Each monomer after the first joins the molecule by one new link, whether on the main chain or a branch: 40 − 1 = 39.
40 links would close a ring somewhere, and the polymer has no rings.
Where a branch starts, one monomer carries an extra bond, but it also starts the branch's first link; the total is still one per added monomer.

why.correct: Atoms are conserved: 2 × C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub> = C<sub>12</sub>H<sub>24</sub>O<sub>12</sub>. The reaction releases one H<sub>2</sub>O, leaving C<sub>12</sub>H<sub>22</sub>O<sub>11</sub>, the formula of table sugar.
options: This is just the two monomers added together. One water molecule (H<sub>2</sub>O) leaves when the bond forms.
Correct. C<sub>12</sub>H<sub>24</sub>O<sub>12</sub> minus H<sub>2</sub>O gives C<sub>12</sub>H<sub>22</sub>O<sub>11</sub>.
This removes two water molecules, but joining two monomers makes one bond and releases one water.
Water leaving takes two hydrogens and one oxygen, not just one oxygen.

why.correct: A polymer is a chain of repeating monomers. Carbohydrates, proteins and nucleic acids fit; lipids do not.
options: Large carbohydrates are chains of sugar monomers, so they are polymers.
Proteins are chains of amino acid monomers.
Nucleic acids are chains of repeating monomers.
Correct. Lipids are built from smaller molecules, but not as long chains of repeating units.

why.correct: In dehydration synthesis one monomer loses –OH and the other loses –H. They combine as H<sub>2</sub>O, and a covalent bond forms between the monomers.
options: The atoms come from both monomers: an –OH from one and an –H from the other.
Correct. Together they make H<sub>2</sub>O, and the two monomers bond where those atoms were.
Splitting water is hydrolysis, which breaks bonds. Dehydration synthesis releases a water molecule.
Enzymes speed up the reaction but do not give their own atoms to the water.

why.correct: Digestion is hydrolysis speeded up by enzymes. Block the enzyme and the polymer stays too big to absorb, so less sugar reaches the blood. (Some real medicines work this way.)
options: Correct. Without hydrolysis the polymer is not cut into monomers, and only small monomers are absorbed.
Large polymers are not absorbed whole; that is why they must be hydrolyzed first.
Dehydration synthesis builds polymers; it does not break them down.
Plenty of water is already present. Without the enzyme, hydrolysis is far too slow to matter.

why.correct: Food proteins are too large to absorb, so they are hydrolyzed into amino acids first. The amino acids travel in the blood to cells, which link them into new proteins by dehydration synthesis.
When monomers are the same, the difference must lie in how they are put together. A different link between monomers changes the chain's shape, and shape decides properties and which enzymes fit.
options: The question states that both are made only of the same monomer.
Correct. Structure determines function: a different link between the same monomers changes the chain's shape, how it packs and which enzymes can cut it.
Chain length alone does not decide this; some very long sugar polymers are digested easily.
Both are polymers, so both were built by dehydration synthesis; hydrolysis breaks polymers down.

why.correct: Reactants are what a reaction starts with; products are what it makes. Hydrolysis: two-monomer molecule + H<sub>2</sub>O → monomer + monomer.
options: The separate monomers are what the reaction produces, the products.
Correct. Hydrolysis uses a water molecule to break the bond, so both are reactants.
Hydrolysis also uses up a water molecule, which is a reactant too.
These are what you get from dehydration synthesis run backwards, but here the monomers are products.

why.correct: A polymer is a chain of many monomers. The protein and the sugar chain qualify; a single sugar, a fat and ATP do not.
options: Polymer: a chain of amino acid monomers joined by covalent bonds.
Not a polymer. A single sugar is a monomer.
Not a polymer. Fats are lipids, built from a few smaller molecules but not as a chain of repeating units.
Polymer: many sugar monomers joined in a chain.
Not a polymer. ATP is one small molecule (with a chain of three phosphate groups, which are not monomers of a polymer).

why.correct: Mass is conserved across the whole reaction, polymer + water → monomers. Because water is a reactant, the monomers contain the water's atoms and weigh more than the polymer alone (about 11.1 g here).
options: That describes dehydration synthesis. In hydrolysis, water is used up and its atoms are added to the monomers.
Hydrolysis rearranges atoms, but it also brings in new atoms from water, so the monomers gain mass.
Correct. Each break adds an –H to one monomer and an –OH to the other, so the monomers outweigh the polymer.
Speed does not change the final atom count: full hydrolysis adds one water per bond however long it takes.

why.correct: Compare each Enzyme B value with its no-enzyme tube. Only cellulose shows a large release; the wood-rotting fungus's enzyme cuts the bonds in cellulose.
options: Enzyme B released 0.3 mg from starch, barely more than the 0.1 mg with no enzyme.
Enzyme B released 0.2 mg from glycogen, about the same as no enzyme.
Substantial: 6.4 mg with Enzyme B against 0.0 mg with no enzyme.
Enzyme B released 0.1 mg from chitin, close to nothing.

why.correct: Same monomer, different glycosidic bond. Enzymes fit the shape of the bond they cut, so a starch-cutting (α) enzyme cannot hydrolyze cellulose's β bonds. Enzyme B, from a fungus that digests wood, can.
options: Both polymers are made entirely of glucose; the difference is in how the glucose units are linked.
Correct. The α or β link holds the chain at a different angle; an enzyme that fits one bond does not fit the other.
Length is not the issue: Enzyme A released almost nothing from cellulose, not a smaller amount.
Cellulose is less soluble, but Enzyme B broke down the same cellulose powder, so the bonds were reachable.

why.correct: Judge two things: is the difference real, and does the design test the proposed cause? With a single tube each and a small gap, the difference could be chance; and branching was never varied, so the data cannot show it is the cause.
options: The difference is small (9.2 versus 7.9 mg) from one tube each; it may not be real, and the data do not test branching at all.
Correct. A claim about a cause needs a real difference and a test of that cause. One tube per treatment shows neither.
Both are made of α-glucose. The flaw is the size of the evidence, not the chemistry.
The no-enzyme tubes show the enzyme is needed; they say nothing about why glycogen gave more sugar than starch.

why.correct: A comparison that lacks only the factor being tested shows what happens without it. Here nearly nothing is released without enzyme, so the sugar in the enzyme tubes comes from enzyme action.
options: Correct. They show the baseline: near zero for all four, so the large values with either enzyme come from the enzymes.
That would need tubes with enzyme but no polysaccharide; these tubes have polysaccharide but no enzyme.
All tubes were run for the same 60 minutes; these tubes never received an enzyme.
All tubes were at 37 °C; testing temperature would need tubes at several temperatures.

why.correct: Wood's energy is locked in cellulose's β-glycosidic bonds. Only enzymes that fit β bonds, made here by gut microbes, can release the glucose.
options: Wood is mostly cellulose. Without microbial enzymes, the termites cannot release its glucose.
Correct. The termites' own small supply of β-cutting enzyme cannot release enough glucose; without the microbes, most of the cellulose stays unusable.
The table shows Enzyme A, a starch-cutting enzyme, releases almost no sugar from cellulose.
Building chitin from wood would first require breaking the cellulose down, which is exactly what they cannot do.

why.correct: α and β glucose are isomers that differ only in whether the carbon-1 –OH points down (α) or up (β).
options: Correct. Everything else in the ring is identical.
Both forms are C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub>, with six carbons.
Both rings contain the same oxygen; the forms differ only at carbon 1.
Both forms contain only C, H and O. Nitrogen is in chitin's sugar, not in β-glucose.

why.correct: β bonds flip every other glucose, so a cellulose chain runs straight. Straight chains pack side by side and hydrogen-bond through their –OH groups into strong fibers.
options: The model shows the reverse: starch chains coil, and cellulose chains are straight.
Correct. Many hydrogen bonds between parallel chains bind them into cables; coiled starch chains cannot line up this way.
The glycosidic bonds run along each chain. The model shows chain-to-chain links as dashed hydrogen bonds.
Both are glucose, with the same –OH groups; and dissolving would weaken fibers, not strengthen them.

why.correct: Combine the model with what you know about elements. Chitin's straight β chains make fibers like cellulose, but its nitrogen means an insect must spend nitrogen to build it.
options: Chitin is β-linked like cellulose, so its chains run straight and form structural fibers.
Starch enzymes fit α bonds; chitin's bonds are β, like cellulose's, so they do not fit.
Correct. Each chitin monomer contains nitrogen, while cellulose contains only C, H and O.
Chitin's sugar units are still joined by glycosidic bonds formed by dehydration synthesis.

why.correct: Every glycosidic bond, α or β, forms by dehydration synthesis: two –OH groups give up H<sub>2</sub>O, and the remaining O bridges the sugars.
options: Hydrolysis breaks glycosidic bonds; it does not form them.
A hydrogen bond is a weak attraction; the link along the chain is a covalent glycosidic bond.
Correct. The –OH groups on carbons 1 and 4 lose the atoms of one water molecule, and the remaining oxygen links the two sugars.
Glycosidic bonds are covalent; neither carbon carries a full charge.

why.correct: Read the peaks: glucose 146, starch 136, sucrose 120, cellulose and water about 88 with no peak.
options: Correct. The glucose drink peaked at 146 mg/dL at 45 minutes; cellulose matched plain water at about 88 mg/dL.
Starch peaked at 136 mg/dL, below glucose's 146, and peaked no earlier.
From 30 minutes on, the starch curve is above the sucrose curve.
Cellulose never rose above the plain-water baseline of about 88 mg/dL.

why.correct: Sucrose = glucose + fructose. Only the glucose half is counted as glucose in the blood, so the same mass of sucrose delivers about half as much glucose.
options: Sucrose did raise glucose in the blood (to 120 mg/dL), so it was digested; humans do hydrolyze sucrose.
Correct. 50 g of sucrose yields roughly 26 g of glucose; the rest is fructose, which this test does not measure as glucose.
Sucrose is a disaccharide, two sugars. A slower breakdown would delay the peak, not shrink it.
Per gram, sucrose holds about as many carbon atoms as glucose; the key is that half of its units are not glucose.

why.correct: Each 342 g of sucrose gives 180 g of glucose. Glucose released = 50 g × 180 ÷ 342 = 26.3 g. (Together with 26.3 g of fructose, that is 52.6 g, more than 50 g, because hydrolysis adds water.)
Free glucose can be absorbed at once. Starch must be hydrolyzed into glucose first, adding a step, so its curve rises more slowly even though it is all glucose.
options: Correct. Only monosaccharides are absorbed. Starch's glycosidic bonds must be cut first, so glucose reaches the blood a little later and less sharply.
Starch is α-glucose. β-glucose polymers (cellulose) are not digested at all.
Starch contains only C, H and O. Per gram it gives slightly more glucose than glucose itself, because hydrolysis adds water.
Polysaccharides are too large to be absorbed; they are hydrolyzed in the gut first.

why.correct: Maltose = glucose + glucose; sucrose = glucose + fructose. Total: three glucose and one fructose.
options: Maltose contains no fructose; it is glucose + glucose.
Correct. Maltose gives two glucose; sucrose gives one glucose and one fructose.
Galactose comes from lactose, not from sucrose or maltose.
Sucrose's second unit is fructose, not glucose.

why.correct: Energy stores: starch in plants, glycogen in animals. Both are α-glucose; glycogen is more branched.
options: Correct. Plants store glucose as starch; animals store it as glycogen, mainly in the liver and muscles.
This reverses them: starch is the plant store, glycogen the animal store.
Cellulose and chitin are structural, not storage, and humans make neither.
Both store α-glucose chains, but animals build them as glycogen, which is more branched.

why.correct: Lactase cuts lactose into glucose and galactose for absorption. With little lactase, lactose stays whole, so less glucose is absorbed and more lactose reaches the large intestine. The molecule itself is unchanged.

variables.name: Amount of lactose reaching the large intestine
variables.why: Without enough lactase, less lactose is hydrolyzed in the small intestine, so more passes on intact.

variables.name: Glucose absorbed into the blood from the milk
variables.why: Glucose is released from lactose only by hydrolysis; less hydrolysis means less glucose to absorb.

variables.name: Number of glucose units in each lactose molecule
variables.why: Lactose is glucose + galactose in everyone; the enzyme level does not change the molecule's structure.

why.correct: Structure predicts function. Straight chains bonded into fibers that enzymes cannot easily break are built for strength, like cellulose and chitin.
options: Storage polysaccharides are coiled and branched so enzymes can release glucose quickly; this one resists starch enzymes.
Correct. Straight, hydrogen-bonded chains make strong fibers, and resistance to digestion suits a long-lasting structure.
Polysaccharides of one repeating sugar carry no information in their order; that is the job of nucleic acids.
Large fibrous chains do not dissolve readily; single sugars are the form carried in blood.

why.correct: Mono- means one. Glucose, fructose and galactose are monosaccharides; sucrose, lactose and maltose are disaccharides; starch, glycogen, cellulose and chitin are polysaccharides.
options: Correct. Fructose is a single six-carbon sugar.
Sucrose is a disaccharide: glucose + fructose.
Glycogen is a polysaccharide of many glucose units.
Lactose is a disaccharide: glucose + galactose.

why.correct: Hold double bonds constant (zero) and compare lengths: each extra two carbons raises the melting point by roughly 7 to 10 °C. Longer straight chains have more length over which to attract their neighbors.
options: Correct. 12, 14, 16 and 18 carbons melt at 44, 54, 63 and 70 °C.
The values go up, not down, from lauric (12 carbons, 44 °C) to stearic (18 carbons, 70 °C).
All four are solid at room temperature, but their melting points still rise steadily with length.
All four melt above about 22 °C, so all four are solid at room temperature.

why.correct: Melting pulls molecules apart, overcoming the attractions between them. A cis kink keeps chains from packing, so there are fewer attractions to overcome.
options: Two hydrogens change the mass by about 1%, far too little to explain 57 °C; elaidic acid has the same formula as oleic acid yet melts at 45 °C.
Correct. Fewer, weaker contacts between bent chains mean less heat is needed to pull them apart.
A C=C double bond is nonpolar; melting point is measured on the pure fatty acid, with no water involved.
Melting separates whole molecules from each other; no covalent bonds inside the chain break.

why.correct: To isolate one factor, compare two molecules that differ only in that factor. Oleic and elaidic acids have identical formulas; only the cis or trans shape differs, and that alone shifts the melting point by 32 °C.
options: Both are saturated; this comparison changes chain length, not shape.
These differ in both the number of hydrogens and the number of kinks, so the two cannot be separated.
Correct. Same length and same number of hydrogens (one double bond each); only the shape differs, cis bent versus trans straight, and the melting points differ by 32 °C.
This changes both the hydrogens and the shape at once, so it cannot show which one matters.

why.correct: A substance is liquid when the room is warmer than its melting point. Of these, only oleic acid (13 °C) qualifies; the others, including trans elaidic acid, melt above 22 °C.
options: Solid: it melts at 44 °C, above room temperature.
Solid: it melts at 63 °C.
Liquid: it melts at 13 °C, below room temperature.
Solid: as a straight trans chain it melts at 45 °C, despite its double bond.
Solid: it melts at 70 °C.

why.correct: Total rise: 70 − 44 = 26 °C. From 12 to 18 carbons is three steps of 2 carbons. 26 ÷ 3 = 8.67, which rounds to 8.7 °C per 2 carbons.
The points fall in a nearly straight line from 68% at 5 °C to 48% at 30 °C, a negative relationship between temperature and unsaturated tails.
options: Correct. The percent falls steadily from 68% at 5 °C to 48% at 30 °C.
This reverses the trend: the highest value (68%) is in the coldest water.
It fell by 20 percentage points, much more than the spread within each group.
The drop is about the same at each step, roughly 4 points per 5 °C.

why.correct: Slope = change in percent ÷ change in temperature = (48 − 68) ÷ (30 − 5) = −20 ÷ 25 = −0.8. The share falls by 0.8 percentage points per °C.

Lower temperature favors tight packing of straight tails, which would stiffen the bilayer. More cis double bonds add kinks that keep the bilayer flexible in the cold, the same reason oils stay liquid when fats set.
options: Goldfish do not warm themselves this way, and the tails measured are in membranes, not fuel stores.
Correct. Cold slows molecules and lets straight tails pack into a stiff, near-solid layer; kinks keep the tails apart.
All groups had the same food. The fish built different membranes, not different diets.
Unsaturated tails are still hydrocarbons and still hydrophobic; a membrane that mixed with water would fall apart.

why.correct: Cold-kept fish build more unsaturated tails. Kinks lower the temperature at which the bilayer stiffens. The basic phospholipid structure, a head and two tails, does not change.

variables.name: Percent of tails that are unsaturated
variables.why: The 5 °C group in the study had about 68% unsaturated tails, against 52% at 25 °C, so the moved fish should shift toward the cold-water value.

variables.name: Temperature at which the membrane lipids would become stiff and gel-like
variables.why: More kinked tails pack less tightly, so the lipids stay flexible to a lower temperature, as oils stay liquid at lower temperatures than fats.

variables.name: Number of fatty acid tails on each phospholipid
variables.why: A phospholipid has two tails whatever the temperature; what changes is which fatty acids fill those positions.

why.correct: A controlled experiment supports a causal claim when the researcher sets the independent variable and holds other variables constant. Here temperature was assigned to groups and food and light were kept the same.
options: Correct. Temperature was the independent variable, set by the researchers, with other conditions held constant, so differences can be credited to it.
A straight-line pattern shows a strong relationship, but a pattern alone, without control of other factors, cannot show cause.
One supplier reduces differences between fish but does not make them identical; the key is that temperature was assigned and other factors held constant.
Larger groups reduce the effect of chance but never remove it; and group size alone does not separate cause from correlation.

why.correct: Amphipathic molecules arrange themselves so that hydrophilic parts touch water and hydrophobic parts touch each other. For a two-tailed phospholipid that is a bilayer, the basis of every cell membrane.
options: Correct. This bilayer keeps the hydrophobic tails away from water and the hydrophilic heads in contact with it.
This would put the hydrophobic tails in contact with water, the arrangement water pushes them out of.
Random orientation would expose tails to water; the molecules arrange themselves to hide them.
The long nonpolar tails keep phospholipids from dissolving as single molecules.

why.correct: Each triglyceride has three fatty acids, each joined to glycerol by one dehydration synthesis that releases one water: 3 waters per triglyceride × 4 = 12.
Fat: 740 ÷ 37 = 20.0 g. Glycogen: 740 ÷ 17 = 43.5 g. Difference: 43.5 − 20.0 = 23.5 g more as glycogen.
Energy per gram depends on what the mass is made of. Fat is nearly all C–H and C–C bonds; a sugar such as glucose is about half oxygen by mass, already bonded to its carbons.
options: Correct. A sugar's carbons each carry oxygen already; a fat's chain is almost pure hydrocarbon, so more of its mass is energy-rich C–H bonds.
Fats are not polymers, and energy per gram depends on the kind of bonds, not on molecule size.
Fatty acids and triglycerides contain no phosphorus; that is in phospholipids, and it is not why fat is energy dense.
Excluding water does not store energy; the energy is in the molecule's chemical bonds.

why.correct: A bilayer needs an amphipathic molecule: a hydrophilic end to face water and a hydrophobic end to hide. Phospholipids have both; triglycerides are almost entirely hydrophobic, so they gather into droplets.
options: Triglycerides are less dense than water (oil floats), and weight does not decide the arrangement.
Correct. With nothing hydrophilic to face outward, triglycerides minimize contact with water by pooling into droplets.
The number of tails is not the problem: with no hydrophilic part, a triglyceride has nothing to place against the water.
Both can be either saturated or unsaturated; how saturated the tails are affects how tightly they pack, not whether a bilayer forms.

why.correct: Steroids are defined by their structure: four fused rings. Their side groups vary, which is how one skeleton gives cholesterol and several different hormones.
options: Correct. Cholesterol, testosterone and estrogen all share this four-ring skeleton.
That describes a triglyceride, a fat or oil.
That describes a phospholipid.
That describes a saturated fatty acid.

why.correct: The middle of a bilayer is a hydrophobic layer of fatty acid tails. Hydrophobic molecules such as steroids dissolve into it and cross; polar and charged molecules are repelled.
options: Small ions such as Na<sup>+</sup> do not pass through the oily middle of a bilayer; chemistry matters, not just size.
Correct. Like dissolves like: the bilayer's core is hydrocarbon, so nonpolar molecules cross it and polar or charged ones do not.
Steroids have no phosphate head; their four-ring skeleton is almost entirely hydrophobic.
Proteins are not hydrolyzed by contact with a membrane; they are kept out by their polarity.

why.correct: Lipids are grouped by being largely hydrophobic: fats and oils (triglycerides), phospholipids and steroids. Polysaccharides and amino acids are polar.
options: Lipid: a steroid, hydrophobic and built on four fused rings.
Not a lipid: a polysaccharide of α-glucose.
Lipid: glycerol plus three fatty acids.
Not a lipid: a polysaccharide of β-glucose.
Lipid: glycerol, two fatty acids and a phosphate head.
Not a lipid: the polar building block of proteins.

why.correct: Compare columns within a row. A matches T and G matches C in each organism, because each A on one strand pairs with a T on the other, and each G with a C.
options: In human DNA A is about 31% and G about 20%, far from equal.
Correct. Within each organism A ≈ T and G ≈ C (human 30.9 and 29.4; 19.9 and 19.8), while the A + T share varies from species to species.
In human DNA A is 30.9% but G is 19.9%; the matching pairs are A with T and G with C.
The percentages differ a lot: A is 24.7% in E. coli but 31.3% in yeast.

why.correct: In double-stranded DNA, %A = %T and %G = %C because the bases pair. A sample that breaks this rule must have unpaired bases: a single strand.
options: Correct. Equal A and T (and G and C) result from base pairing between two strands. Virus X's 24.0% A versus 31.2% T shows its DNA is not paired.
The table reports thymine for Virus X (31.2%), so its nucleic acid has T, not U.
More hydrogen bonds would not break the A = T rule; in any double-stranded DNA, A pairs with T.
Size does not make the measurement unreliable; the pattern is consistent with a real structural difference.

why.correct: G pairs with C, so C = 21% and G + C = 42%. A + T = 100 − 42 = 58%, and A = T, so A = 29%.
Complementary base pairing: each A sits opposite a T. Count the bases on both strands and every pair adds one A and one T, so %A = %T.
options: The amounts in DNA are set by pairing, not by how fast free bases are made; single-stranded Virus X shows unequal A and T.
Correct. Every base pair contributes one A and one T (or one G and one C), so the totals are equal however the pairs are arranged.
The backbone links sugars and phosphates along a strand; A and T are linked across the two strands by hydrogen bonds.
A and T have different formulas and shapes; they are partners in pairing, not isomers.

why.correct: Two facts: RNA uses U instead of T, and equal amounts of partner bases arise only from pairing between two strands. A single-stranded RNA need not show it.
options: Correct. RNA uses uracil, and in a single strand there is no partner strand to force A to equal U.
RNA contains uracil instead of thymine, not in addition to it.
A and U pair only where two strands (or folded parts of one strand) meet; a single strand need not have equal A and U.
RNA lacks thymine; and %G = %C is a feature of double strands.

why.correct: The points form a straight rising line, a positive relationship: more G + C, higher separation temperature.
options: Correct. The points rise in a nearly straight line from 81.6 °C at 30% G + C to 97.2 °C at 68%.
The temperatures rise, not fall, as G + C content goes up.
The rise continues past 52%: 90.6, then 93.9, then 97.2 °C.
They span almost 16 °C, from 81.6 to 97.2 °C.

why.correct: Slope = (97.2 − 81.6) ÷ (68 − 30) = 15.6 ÷ 38 = 0.41 °C per percentage point of G + C.
Separating strands means breaking the hydrogen bonds between paired bases. Three per G–C pair against two per A–T pair: the more G–C pairs, the more heat needed.
options: Correct. More hydrogen bonds per pair means more attraction holding the strands together. (Base stacking adds to this too; see the notes.)
All base pairs are held by hydrogen bonds; covalent bonds are inside each strand.
Mass does not set the separation temperature; the attraction between paired bases does.
The backbone stays intact when strands separate; heating breaks the hydrogen bonds between bases.

why.correct: Read between the 45% and 52% points (87.8 and 90.6 °C). Or use the line: 81.6 + 0.41 × (50 − 30) ≈ 89.8 °C.
options: 84 °C fits a G + C content near 36%, well below 50%.
Correct. 50% lies between the 45% and 52% points (87.8 and 90.6 °C), so about 90 °C.
95 °C fits about 62% G + C.
100 °C is beyond the highest point, which is 97.2 °C at 68%.

why.correct: Separate what the data show (a test-tube property of DNA) from the claim (a pattern in nature). A claim about where organisms live needs data about those organisms; cells also have other ways to protect their DNA.
options: The data show how purified DNA behaves when heated; they include no hot-spring bacteria and say nothing about where these species live.
Correct. Testing the claim would need G + C contents of bacteria from hot springs and from cooler places. (Surveys of real species find little link for whole DNA content.)
The data do show an effect of G + C content, so this part is wrong.
High values exist among the six, but nothing links those species to hot habitats.

why.correct: Strands are antiparallel. Read Strand 2 from its 5′ end, which is on the right: G A A T G C C A T.
options: These are Strand 2's bases read left to right, which is its 3′ to 5′ direction. Written 5′ to 3′, the order must be reversed.
Correct. Strand 2 runs 3′-TACCGTAAG-5′; reversed to start at its 5′ end, it reads 5′-GAATGCCAT-3′.
This is Strand 1's sequence, not its partner.
This is Strand 1 reversed without pairing the bases.

why.correct: Strand 1 is A T G G C A T T C. Positions 1, 2, 6, 7 and 8 are A–T pairs: 5 × 2 = 10. Positions 3, 4, 5 and 9 are G–C pairs: 4 × 3 = 12. Total 10 + 12 = 22.
Strand direction comes from the sugar's numbered carbons: a free phosphate on carbon 5′ marks the 5′ end; a free –OH on carbon 3′ marks the 3′ end.
options: Correct. The 5′ end of a strand has a free phosphate attached to the 5′ carbon of its sugar.
The 3′ end has a free –OH on the 3′ carbon, where new nucleotides would be added.
Every nucleotide has a phosphate, but inside the strand each one links two sugars; only at the 5′ end is one left free.
Phosphates link sugars to sugars in the backbone; the bases are attached to carbon 1′.

why.correct: RNA uses the same A, G and C as DNA, with U in place of T. Matching Strand 1: ATGGCATTC becomes AUGGCAUUC.
options: Correct. Every T becomes U; A, G and C stay the same.
RNA does not use thymine; each T must be uracil.
This is the complement of Strand 1 with U for T; the RNA was meant to match Strand 1, not pair with it.
Only T changes to U. Changing A to U (or the order of bases) gives a different sequence.

why.correct: Nucleotide = phosphate + pentose (five-carbon sugar) + nitrogenous base.
options: Correct. These three parts make up every DNA and RNA nucleotide.
These are the parts of an amino acid, the monomer of proteins.
These make up a phospholipid, a lipid.
Nucleotides contain a five-carbon sugar (ribose or deoxyribose), not a six-carbon sugar.

why.correct: The two chemical differences are the sugar (ribose versus deoxyribose) and one base (uracil versus thymine). Backbones, strand direction and A, G, C are shared.
options: RNA only. DNA uses deoxyribose, which lacks the –OH on carbon 2′.
Both have sugar-phosphate backbones.
RNA only. DNA uses thymine in its place.
Both: every nucleic acid strand has a direction.
Both use guanine.

why.correct: Two kinds of bonds, two strengths: weak hydrogen bonds across the helix (broken by moderate heat), strong covalent bonds along each strand (unbroken).
options: Correct. Hydrogen bonds are weak attractions; the covalent bonds of the sugar-phosphate backbone need far more energy to break.
This reverses the bonds: hydrogen bonds join the base pairs, covalent bonds hold the backbone.
If the backbone broke, each strand would fall apart into nucleotides, not stay one long chain.
The phosphates do repel, at any temperature; the change with heating is that the hydrogen bonds between bases break.

why.correct: Information is carried by the order of bases, not by how many of each there are. Two molecules with the same composition can have entirely different sequences.
options: Percentages say nothing about order; information is in the sequence.
Correct. Like words made of the same letters, molecules with the same base counts can have completely different sequences.
Pairing links the two strands of one molecule; it does not force two different molecules to have the same order.
Genes can have the same percentages; what makes them different is their sequences.

why.correct: Compare versions that differ in one thing. At position 45, a similar swap (V1) kept 96% while a charged one (V2) left 3%. At the surface even a charge reversal (V4) kept 91%.
options: Correct. V1 and V3 (similar chemistry) kept 96% and 99%; V2 (a charge placed in the core) fell to 3%.
Activity ranged from 3% to 99%, so the effects were very different.
The surface changes (V3, V4) kept 99% and 91%, more than any core change except the similar swap in V1.
That swap (V4) kept 91% of activity, among the smallest effects.

why.correct: R-group chemistry drives folding. Nonpolar side chains pack into the core by hydrophobic interactions. A charged side chain there is out of place, so the protein folds differently and loses its working shape.
options: Correct. The core is held together by nonpolar side chains clustering away from water; a charge there is unstable and disrupts the tertiary structure.
Swapping a side chain does not break the backbone; V2 is still one intact polypeptide.
Each version still has 240 amino acids. The problem is chemistry, a charge in a nonpolar region, not length.
Disulfide bridges form between two cysteines; aspartic acid has no sulfhydryl group.

why.correct: A disulfide bridge is a covalent bond between two cysteine sulfhydryl groups. Replace one cysteine with serine and the bridge is lost, so the fold it held is free to shift.
options: Dissolving would not break peptide bonds; the chain stays intact. The loss is in the shape.
Correct. Two –SH groups are needed for an S–S bridge. Losing the bridge leaves the tertiary structure less stable.
Every amino acid forms peptide bonds through its amino and carboxyl groups; the side chain does not take part.
A disulfide bridge needs sulfur on both sides; serine has oxygen, not sulfur.

why.correct: Position 45 sits in the nonpolar core. The safest replacement keeps the side chain nonpolar; V1 shows that such a swap barely changes activity.
options: A charge buried in the core would disrupt folding, as V2 shows.
This is nearly the same change as V2, which left 3% activity.
Correct. A nonpolar side chain fits the hydrophobic core, as isoleucine did in V1.
A polar group buried in the core is less disruptive than a charge but still does not fit the hydrophobic environment.

why.correct: To test the effect of position, compare two changes that are chemically alike but at different positions. V2 and V4 both introduce a negative side chain; the core change is devastating, the surface change mild.
options: Both are at the same position, so this pair tests how different the new side chain is, not where the change is.
Both are at the same surface position; again only the side chain differs.

Correct. Both put a negative side chain in place, and V4's change (positive to negative) is if anything the bigger one, yet it kept 91% at the surface while V2 kept 3% in the core. Position made the difference.
These differ in both position and kind of change, and their similar activities do not separate the two factors.

why.correct: Urea and the reducing agent break the bonds of secondary and tertiary structure. With its shape gone, the enzyme does not work.
options: Correct. Activity fell from 100% to less than 1% when the bonds holding its shape were broken.
Neither breaks peptide bonds; Sample C regains activity from the same chains, which could not happen if they had been cut up.
Activity dropped to less than 1%, so shape is essential.
In B the activity is less than 1%, not about half.

why.correct: If an unfolded chain refolds and works again with nothing else added, the instructions for its shape must be in the chain itself: sequence determines shape.
options: Correct. With only the chain itself present and normal conditions restored, it regained 95% of its activity.
Activity returned when urea was removed; urea unfolds the enzyme.
No chaperones were present in C, yet the enzyme refolded on its own.
Sample D shows that bridges formed in the wrong places keep activity at 1%, so they matter a great deal.

why.correct: In D the bridges re-formed while the chain was unfolded, so cysteines paired at random. Wrong covalent bridges hold the chain in wrong shapes; a trace of reducing agent, as in Sample E, lets them break and re-form until the correct shape wins.
options: Sample E, made from D, recovered 90% of its activity, so its chains were intact.
Correct. Covalent bridges formed before folding fix whatever pairings happen; most random pairings are wrong.
Urea does not break or rearrange peptide bonds; E shows the chain could still fold correctly.
All 8 cysteines are still present; D's bridges formed, but in the wrong places.

why.correct: 7 × 5 × 3 × 1 = 105. Only one set is correct, so random pairing gives the right bridges about 1 time in 105, roughly 1%, matching Sample D's activity.
Denaturing treatments break the weak bonds of secondary and tertiary structure (and disulfides, with a reducing agent), but peptide bonds survive, so the primary structure remains.
options: Correct. The sequence survives, which is why the chains can refold in C.
Helices and sheets are held by hydrogen bonds, which urea breaks.
Urea breaks hydrophobic interactions, and activity is lost, so the 3-D shape is gone.
The enzyme is a single chain of 124 amino acids, so it has no quaternary structure.

why.correct: Amino acids share a common core; the R group gives each one its chemistry: nonpolar, polar or charged.
options: Correct. The amino group, carboxyl group, hydrogen and central carbon are the same in all 20; only the R group differs.
Every amino acid has one amino group on its central carbon (some side chains carry extra nitrogen, but that is part of the R group).
All amino acids link by the same peptide bond.
All amino acids contain carbon.

why.correct: Dehydration synthesis: –OH from the carboxyl group and –H from the amino group leave as water; the carbonyl carbon bonds to the nitrogen, forming C–N, the peptide bond.
options: Correct. The carboxyl group loses –OH, the amino group loses –H, water is released, and C bonds to N.
R groups interact during folding, but the peptide bond is in the backbone, between carboxyl and amino groups.
The central carbons are not bonded to each other; they are linked through the C–N peptide bond.
A peptide bond links a carboxyl carbon to an amino nitrogen, not two nitrogens.

why.correct: Secondary structure (α helices and β sheets) is held by hydrogen bonds between the backbone's C=O and N–H groups. Side-chain interactions belong to tertiary structure.
options: Correct. Secondary structure depends on the backbone, not the side chains.
Disulfide bridges stabilize tertiary structure and need two cysteines; most helices have none.
Peptide bonds link neighboring amino acids along the chain, not every fourth one.
Side chains point outward from a helix; hydrophobic interactions shape the tertiary structure.

why.correct: Primary structure is the sequence of amino acids. Only changing which amino acids are in the chain (or their order) changes it; denaturing and folding act on the higher levels.
options: Changes primary structure: the sequence itself is different.
Does not: heat breaks weak bonds, not peptide bonds, so the sequence is unchanged.
Does not: pH changes charges on side chains and can unfold the protein, but the sequence stays the same.
Does not: disulfide bridges are part of tertiary structure.
Does not: chaperones help folding; they do not change the sequence.

why.correct: A surface position normally faces water, where a charged side chain fits well. A nonpolar side chain there creates a sticky hydrophobic spot that binds neighboring molecules.
options: Correct. A hydrophobic patch exposed to water binds other hydrophobic surfaces, stacking hemoglobin into fibers when oxygen is low.
A side-chain swap does not break the backbone; the chain stays full length.
Glutamic acid has no sulfhydryl group, so no disulfide bridge is lost.
Valine is nonpolar and uncharged; the problem is extra stickiness, not repulsion.

why.correct: Denaturation breaks the weak bonds of secondary and tertiary structure but not peptide bonds. Unfolding exposes hydrophobic side chains, which clump with other chains, so the protein does not refold on cooling.

variables.name: Number of peptide bonds in each chain
variables.why: Cooking temperatures do not break peptide bonds; the sequence of each chain is unchanged.

variables.name: Number of hydrogen bonds holding helices and sheets
variables.why: Heat makes the chain vibrate hard enough to break these weak bonds, so secondary structure is lost.

variables.name: Number of nonpolar side chains exposed to water
variables.why: As the chain unfolds, nonpolar side chains that were buried in the core are exposed; they then stick to other unfolded chains, turning the egg white solid and white.

why.correct: Heat unfolds proteins and exposes hydrophobic regions that clump. Chaperones shield those regions and help chains refold into working shapes.
options: Correct. Chaperones bind partly unfolded chains, keep their exposed nonpolar regions from sticking to each other, and give them a chance to refold.
Breaking proteins into amino acids is hydrolysis; chaperones assist folding.
Chaperones do not change sequences; the sequence is set by the gene.
Chaperones help other proteins fold; they do not take over their functions.

why.correct: Primary (sequence) → secondary (helices from backbone hydrogen bonds) → tertiary (folding driven by side chains) → quaternary (four subunits together). Each level depends on the one before.
In water, a folding chain hides its nonpolar side chains inside and exposes its polar and charged ones, the same hydrophobic effect that makes oil form drops.
options: Nonpolar side chains do not help a protein dissolve; water-soluble proteins have mostly polar and charged surfaces.
Correct. Hydrophobic interactions pack nonpolar side chains into the core, leaving polar and charged ones on the water-facing surface.
Folding sorts side chains by chemistry, not evenly; nonpolar ones gather inside.
Only cysteines form disulfide bridges; leucine and valine have no sulfur.
